title: The keeper of the light
text:
The school radio club interviews Mr Okafor, a retired lighthouse keeper who visited the school for Local History Week.

INES: Good morning, Mr Okafor, and thank you for joining us. Please tell our listeners what your job was.

MR OKAFOR: Good morning, Ines. For twenty-six years I looked after a lighthouse on a rocky headland. My main duty was to make sure the light shone every single night, so that ships could steer away from the rocks.

INES: Was the light always electric?

MR OKAFOR: No, not at first. When I began, the lamp burned oil, and I had to climb ninety-three steps each evening to light it. A great glass lens, taller than me, gathered the flame and sent it out in a long beam. The whole lens turned slowly, so sailors saw a flash every ten seconds. Each lighthouse has its own pattern, so a captain can tell exactly where he is.

INES: That sounds very lonely. Did you live there by yourself?

MR OKAFOR: (laughing) Not quite. My wife and I lived in the cottage beside the tower, and our two children went to school by boat on Mondays and came home on Fridays. But yes, some winter nights were very quiet. When the fog came down I had to sound the horn every thirty seconds, even if I had not slept.

INES: Did anything frightening ever happen?

MR OKAFOR: Once, in a storm, a fishing boat lost its engine and drifted towards the rocks. I could not rescue it myself, so I called the coastguard on the radio and kept the light shining as brightly as I could. They towed the boat to safety at dawn. Four fishermen shook my hand that morning, and I never forgot it.

INES: Is that why you loved the work?

MR OKAFOR: Partly. I liked knowing that people I would never meet were safe because of me. Then, in the end, machines took over. Today the light switches on by itself, and a technician visits twice a year.

INES: Do you miss it?

MR OKAFOR: Every evening, when the sun goes down, I still look at the clock. Old habits stay with you.

INES: Thank you, Mr Okafor. That was the radio club, signing off for today.
